title: Columbus and the Eclipse
text:
On his fourth voyage, in June 1503, Christopher Columbus was stranded on the north coast of Jamaica. His two remaining ships were so riddled by shipworm that he had them run aground. A few of his men set off by canoe to seek help from Hispaniola, but months passed without rescue.

At first the local Taino people traded food for trinkets. As time went on, they grew tired of feeding a hundred hungry strangers, and some of Columbus's men mutinied and robbed villages. The supplies dwindled.

Columbus's son Ferdinand, who was with him, describes what happened next. Columbus had an astronomical almanac which predicted a total lunar eclipse for the night of 29 February 1504. He called the local chiefs together and told them that God was angry at their refusal to feed his people and would show it by a sign in the sky that night. As the moon rose, it darkened and turned red. The Taino, frightened, begged Columbus to intercede. He withdrew to his cabin, timed the eclipse, and shortly before it ended, announced that God had forgiven them on condition that they supply food. The moon returned to normal.

From then on, Ferdinand writes, the Taino provided food willingly. A rescue ship finally arrived in June 1504, and Columbus returned to Spain.
lesson: Knowledge others lack is a form of power. Notice how easily it can be used to manipulate, and judge such tricks by who benefits and at whose expense.
source: Ferdinand Columbus, The Life of the Admiral Christopher Columbus by His Son Ferdinand
